source.title: Refusal Before Decoding: Detecting and Exploiting Refusal Signals in Intermediate LLM Activations
source.authors: M. G. Collu; Riccardo Conte; A. Giaretta; Denis Kleyko; Mauro Conti; Matteo Zavatteri; Roberto Confalonieri

record.tranche_reason: The study trains linear probes on intermediate residual-stream activations and reports held-out refusal-label accuracy, a conceptual test of whether refusal-related information is linearly decodable. It does not use the original difference-in-means direction or causally intervene on it.
record.gate_note: The probe-accuracy results bear on the decodability aspect of V1. The study does not test whether ablating or adding a single direction changes refusals or preserves other abilities. Mechanistic AutoDAN attack success, transfer, and opposite-objective results evaluate the study's probe-guided search method; they do not measure suppression of the claimed direction and are not rows for the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains supervised LR and MLP probes to predict a refusal label from last-token residual activations, then uses probe scores as the fitness signal in a jailbreak search. It never computes a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. It never ablates or adds any direction, and never measures refusal rates under intervention. The authors say high probe accuracy 'does not by itself establish that the model causally uses' the feature. Decodability is a related but different construct from V1's causal mediation, so it goes under fits_no_version. The attack results evaluate the authors' own method. The study does not measure whether jailbreaks suppress a refusal direction, so they do not bear on V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also report that reversing the probe objective barely changes ASR on the 3B/4B models. So on those models the probe signal adds little, and it is informative mainly on the 27B model. They also find held-out probe accuracy a weak layer-selection criterion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised linear classifiers trained on prompt-label pairs and last-token residual activations, rather than a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means vector. No direction ablation or addition is performed.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe accuracy varies with layer and classifier architecture, although the authors report generally similar, high accuracy across layers. Their post-hoc maximum-block selection is descriptive and also informs attack-block selection.

fits_no_version.finding: LR and MLP probes decode a refusable-vs-compliant prompt label from last-token residual activations, at .88-.89 at block 1 and ~.97-.99+ by middle blocks, in all three models. Linear and MLP probes perform similarly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A prompt's refusal class is linearly decodable from early-to-middle residual-stream activations (decodability, not causal mediation).

record.problems: Probe accuracy is a decodability measure, not evidence of causal mediation. The authors note that the post-hoc best accuracy is selected after comparing layers on the held-out split; probes are model-specific; dataset labels may be model-dependent; and the model/sample coverage is limited. No causal intervention or general-capability test is reported.
record.rows_left_out: The remaining per-layer LR and MLP accuracy results in Appendix D, Tables 10-11, are omitted due to the 60-row limit. Selected rows retain early, intermediate, post-hoc high-accuracy, and last-listed-layer examples across the three models.

untested.parts: No diff-in-means direction, no ablation or addition, no refusal-rate change, no capability check.
Never measures whether jailbreak prompts suppress a refusal direction; no adversarial training.
Harm and refusal labels are conflated; refusable set is filtered harmful prompts.
Only prompt transfer is tested; probes are stated to be model-specific.
Qwen-3.6-27B emits think tags, but no direction intervention is tested.

record.verdict_notes: Record values for R39, R40, R57 and R58 are misread from Table 10. The refusal label comes from dataset-level harmful vs Alpaca prompts filtered by one aligned model, not per-model refusal behaviour. The authors note the label may be partly model-dependent. Reader's V1 'supports' label removed: decodability is not the V1 claim.

versions.untested_parts: Tests linear decodability of refusal labels from residual-stream activations, not the original harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, causal mediation, ablation at every layer and position, addition, or preservation of other abilities.
No weight edit or abliteration experiment.
The attack uses probe scores to rank prompt candidates; it does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No test of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Prompt transfer across models is evaluated, but not transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or stages.
No test of whether the claimed causal mechanism holds in reasoning models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Linear-probe refusal-label decodability at the reported layers in all three evaluated models
reader_labels.reason: Held-out accuracy is high at early-to-middle blocks, consistent with refusal-relevant information being linearly accessible before the final layer; this does not establish the claimed causal mediation. Rows R01-R60.
